Content:
Suppose that [MATH: f(x,y) = x y^2 - x^3 y.] Then the first-order partial derivatives are
[MATH: \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} (x,y) = y^2 -3x^2y \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x,y) = 2xy -x^3,]

Content:
and the second-order mixed partial derivatives are
[MATH: \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\, \partial x}(x,y) = 2y -3x^2 \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\, \partial y}(x,y) = 2y-3x^2.]

Content:
Notice that these two mixed partial derivatives are equal, i.e.,
[MATH: \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\, \partial x}=\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\, \partial y}.]

Content:
In general, if a function [MATH: f(x,y)] has continuous first-order partial derivatives on an open set [MATH: U,] and the second-order mixed partial derivatives exist and are continuous on [MATH: U,] then the mixed partial derivatives are equal everywhere on [MATH: U.]

items.title: Finding Missing Constants in First-Order Partial Derivative Expressions

sections.normalized_html: Suppose that the function [MATH: f(x,y)] and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set [MATH: U.] Find the values of [MATH: a] and [MATH: b,] if [MATH: f_x(x,y) = 6xy+axy^3-5, \qquad f_y(x,y) = 3x^2+bx^2y^2, \qquad f_y(2,-1) = -24.]
sections.readable_text:
Suppose that the function [MATH: f(x,y)] and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set [MATH: U.] Find the values of [MATH: a] and [MATH: b,] if
[MATH: f_x(x,y) = 6xy+axy^3-5, \qquad
f_y(x,y) = 3x^2+bx^2y^2, \qquad
f_y(2,-1) = -24.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we compute the mixed partial derivatives: [MATH: f_{xy}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(f_{x}(x, y)); = (∂)/(∂y)(6xy + axy^{3} − 5); = 6x + 3axy^{2} − 0; = 6x + 3axy^{2}; f_{yx}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂x)(f_{y}(x, y)); = (∂)/(∂x)(3x^{2} + bx^{2}y^{2}); = 6x + 2bxy^{2}]

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set [MATH: U,] the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. So, we have the identity

[MATH: f_{xy}(x, y)|= f_{yx}(x, y); 6x + 3axy^{2}|= 6x + 2bxy^{2}.]

Equating the coefficients of [MATH: xy^2,] we see that [MATH: 3a=2b.]

Now, since [MATH: f_y(2,-1)=-24,] we get [MATH: f_{y}(2, − 1)|= − 24; 3(2)^{2} + b(2)^{2}(− 1)^{2}|= − 24; 12 + 4b|= − 24; 4b|= − 36; b|= − 9]

Finally, [MATH: 3a|= 2b; 3a|= 2(− 9); 3a|= − 18; a|= − 6.]

Therefore, [MATH: a=-6] and [MATH: b=-9.]

items.title: Identifying Possible Pairs of First-Order Partial Derivatives

sections.normalized_html:
Suppose that the function [MATH: f(x,y)] and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set [MATH: U.] Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of [MATH: f(x,y)?]

  1. [MATH: f_x(x,y)=x+2y] and [MATH: f_y(x,y)=2y-x]

  2. [MATH: f_x(x,y)=5(x+y)^4] and [MATH: f_y(x,y)=5(x+y)^4]

  3. [MATH: f_x(x,y)=-\sin{x}\sin{y}] and [MATH: f_y(x,y)=\cos{x}\cos{y}]
sections.readable_text:
Suppose that the function [MATH: f(x,y)] and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set [MATH: U.] Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of [MATH: f(x,y)?]

1. [MATH: f_x(x,y)=x+2y] and [MATH: f_y(x,y)=2y-x]
2. [MATH: f_x(x,y)=5(x+y)^4] and [MATH: f_y(x,y)=5(x+y)^4]
3. [MATH: f_x(x,y)=-\sin{x}\sin{y}] and [MATH: f_y(x,y)=\cos{x}\cos{y}]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set [MATH: U,] the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, [MATH: f_{xy}(x,y)=f_{yx}(x,y).] Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

  • For the first pair, the mixed partial derivatives are [MATH: f_{xy}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(x + 2y) = 2,; f_{yx}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂x)(2y − x) = − 1.] Since [MATH: f_{xy}(x,y) \neq f_{yx}(x,y),] the first pair could not represent the first-order partial derivatives of [MATH: f(x,y).]

  • For the second pair, the mixed partial derivatives are [MATH: f_{xy}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(5(x + y)^{4}) = 20(x + y)^{3},; f_{yx}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂x)(5(x + y)^{4}) = 20(x + y)^{3}.] Since [MATH: f_{xy}(x,y) = f_{yx}(x,y),] the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of [MATH: f(x,y).]

  • For the third pair, the mixed partial derivatives are [MATH: f_{xy}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(− \sin x\sin y) = − \sin x\cos y,; f_{yx}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂x)(\cos x\cos y) = − \sin x\cos y.] Since [MATH: f_{xy}(x,y)=f_{yx}(x,y),] the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of [MATH: f(x,y).]

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: f(x,y) = x y^2 - x^3 y.] Then the first-order partial derivatives are
[MATH: \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} (x,y) = y^2 -3x^2y \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x,y) = 2xy -x^3,]

Content:
and the second-order mixed partial derivatives are
[MATH: \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\, \partial x}(x,y) = 2y -3x^2 \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\, \partial y}(x,y) = 2y-3x^2.]

Content:
Notice that these two mixed partial derivatives are equal, i.e.,
[MATH: \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\, \partial x}=\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\, \partial y}.]

Content:
In general, if a function [MATH: f(x,y)] has continuous first-order partial derivatives on an open set [MATH: U,] and the second-order mixed partial derivatives exist and are continuous on [MATH: U,] then the mixed partial derivatives are equal everywhere on [MATH: U.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding Missing Constants in First-Order Partial Derivative Expressions

Example Prompt:
Suppose that the function [MATH: f(x,y)] and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set [MATH: U.] Find the values of [MATH: a] and [MATH: b,] if
[MATH: f_x(x,y) = 6xy+axy^3-5, \qquad
f_y(x,y) = 3x^2+bx^2y^2, \qquad
f_y(2,-1) = -24.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we compute the mixed partial derivatives:
[MATH: f_{xy}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(f_{x}(x, y)); = (∂)/(∂y)(6xy + axy^{3} − 5); = 6x + 3axy^{2} − 0; = 6x + 3axy^{2}; f_{yx}(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂x)(f_{y}(x, y)); = (∂)/(∂x)(3x^{2} + bx^{2}y^{2}); = 6x + 2bxy^{2}]

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set [MATH: U,] the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. So, we have the identity

[MATH: f_{xy}(x, y)|= f_{yx}(x, y); 6x + 3axy^{2}|= 6x + 2bxy^{2}.]

Equating the coefficients of [MATH: xy^2,] we see that [MATH: 3a=2b.]

Now, since [MATH: f_y(2,-1)=-24,] we get
[MATH: f_{y}(2, − 1)|= − 24; 3(2)^{2} + b(2)^{2}(− 1)^{2}|= − 24; 12 + 4b|= − 24; 4b|= − 36; b|= − 9]

Finally,
[MATH: 3a|= 2b; 3a|= 2(− 9); 3a|= − 18; a|= − 6.]

Therefore, [MATH: a=-6] and [MATH: b=-9.]
